title: PRESIDENT OF INDIA HOSTS HEREDITARY PRINCE ALOIS AND PRINCESS SOPHIE OF LIECHTENSTEIN
subtitle: WE CAN DEVELOP A MUTUALLY BENEFICIAL PARTNERSHIP BY COMBINING LIECHTENSTEIN’S EXPERTISE IN THE FIELDS OF ADVANCED MANUFACTURING, INNOVATION, AND FINANCIAL SERVICES WITH INDIA’S SKILLED WORKFORCE, MANUFACTURING CAPACITY, AND RAPIDLY GROWING MARKET: PRESIDENT DROUPADI MURMU
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 9:57PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The President of India, Smt. Droupadi Murmu received H.S.H. Hereditary Prince Alois and H.R.H. Hereditary Princess Sophie of Liechtenstein at Rashtrapati Bhavan today (October 27, 2026). She also hosted a banquet in their honour.
Welcoming Hereditary Prince Alois and his delegation to India, the President said that his regular engagement and connection with India reflect his long-standing commitment to bilateral relations between India and Liechtenstein.
The President was happy to note that cooperation between India and Liechtenstein continues to grow across sectors such as trade, investment, science and technology, innovation, culture, and people-to-people ties. She said that in the present uncertain geopolitical and geoeconomic landscape, strengthening the economic partnership between the two countries has become more important than ever.
The President said that the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement between India and the European Free Trade Association, which was concluded in 2024, has opened up new avenues to deepen our trade and investment relations. She expressed confidence that the commitment to facilitate $100 billion in investments in India and create 1 million direct jobs over the next 15 years will provide a robust foundation for expanding cooperation across our shared priorities.
The President was happy to note that various companies from Liechtenstein are showing a keen interest in expanding their collaboration with India in sectors such as advanced manufacturing, Fintech, agricultural research, sustainable infrastructure, healthcare, and material sciences. She added that there is significant potential for skill development and vocational training, particularly through the promotion of partnerships between industry and educational institutions.
She said that by combining Liechtenstein’s expertise in the fields of advanced manufacturing, innovation, and financial services with India’s skilled workforce, manufacturing capacity, and rapidly growing market, we can develop a mutually beneficial partnership.
The two leaders agreed that close cooperation between India and Liechtenstein can bring immense benefits to our people. They also agreed that this visit will contribute to further strengthening relations between the two countries.

title: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurates Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave 2026
subtitle:
A Viksit Bharat will be built on strong foundations of scientific research, discoveries and the spirit of innovation: PM

India must innovate and lead the world in shaping the technologies of tomorrow: PM

India aims to achieve self-reliance and build strength in critical technologies: PM

AI can give quick answers, but it is essential to verify them: PM
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 7:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurated the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave 2026 today at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. Addressing the Conclave, the Prime Minister shared his enthusiasm following a lively interaction with startup founders earlier in the day. He praised the expansive vision and bold determination of the nation's youth. “The scale at which the youth of India are thinking and the self-confidence with which they are moving forward is encouraging,” remarked Shri Modi.
Recalling his participation in the previous edition of the Conclave, the Prime Minister contrasted past decades,when India merely played catch-up by adopting or modifying foreign innovations years later, with the new mindset of 21st-century India that aims to create original technologies, set global directions, and solve worldwide challenges. Citing how the nation developed indigenous COVID-19 vaccines to inoculate its population and supply other nations, alongside reaching Mars on its maiden attempt and landing on the uncharted lunar South Pole, he outlined a bold technological vision for the country."India must embrace the technologies of the future, innovate boldly, and lead the world in creating them,” asserted PM Modi.
Highlighting India’s rich heritage of discovery ranging from the invention of Zero and the number system to astronomy, the Prime Minister noted that the country is advancing this scientific legacy with modern technology and renewed confidence, as demonstrated by several milestones over the past year. With the nation set to celebrate the birth anniversary of Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha on October 30, he chose to begin his review of recent breakthroughs with the nuclear sector."Therefore, let us begin with Nuclear Energy,” remarked Shri Modi.
Emphasizing that building a Viksit Bharat requires massive nuclear energy capacity while reliance on imported nuclear fuel poses a challenge to energy security, the Prime Minister pointed out that the nation is rapidly advancing its Fast Breeder Reactor technology. He highlighted that just a few months ago, the indigenous 500-Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor successfully achieved First Criticality. "This has been a major step in the direction of strengthening our Long Term Strengths in the field of Nuclear Energy,” noted PM Modi.
Stating that India's ambition extends beyond domestic energy security and technological self-reliance to expanding its footprint across critical technologies, the Prime Minister highlighted major space sector achievements this year, including an Indian space startup placing a satellite into orbit on its maiden attempt using a Made-in-India rocket and the country mastering satellite docking capability. He added that numerous domestic startups are introducing novel space science solutions alongside growing participation from young scientists and entrepreneurs. "Our goal is also to expand our power in Critical Technologies,” asserted Shri Modi.
Describing the sheer breadth of India's multi-sectoral achievements as unprecedented, the Prime Minister noted that this year the country hosted the AI Impact Summit, launched its own AI Model, and began shipping India-made semiconductor chips to the world. He also pointed out that the nation is actively building battery storage capacity anchored entirely in domestically available raw materials. "The diverse sectors in which India is achieving successes is unprecedented,” observed PM Modi.
Observing that while sectors ranging from nuclear and space to AI and semiconductors have distinct requirements, they collectively signal India's rising strength and confidence in emerging technologies, the Prime Minister spotlighted the nation's unique capacity to deliver 'Solution at Scale' so that domestic breakthroughs can solve global challenges. Pointing to the success of the Digital Stack and indigenous 5G technology, he emphasized the ongoing drive to build secure, population-scale platforms. "India is moving forward in the direction of developing such Secure Solutions which can reach people on a large scale,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Contrasting the historical tendency to view science and technology as weapons with India's philosophy of using them to serve humanity, the Prime Minister stated that true scientific success lies in stepping out of the lab to improve ordinary lives, solve massive problems, and strengthen healthcare, agriculture, education, employment, and disaster resilience. Expressing satisfaction that Indian startups are prioritizing these areas, he cited startups and domestic firms working on wearable EEG technology to understand brain activity, indigenous wireless and satellite communications, specialized nutritional products, new semiconductor technologies, and solutions to utilize industrial waste like steel slag. "The real success of Science occurs when it steps out of the lab and makes the life of the common citizen better,” asserted PM Modi.
Sharing his recent experience at IIT Madras in Chennai, the Prime Minister recalled inaugurating a modern Brain Centre that has created a globally exemplary brain imaging technology platform to develop high-resolution digital 3D images of the human brain and unravel complex neurological diseases. He declared that 'Science for Society' and 'Technology for Transformation' must serve as the ultimate benchmark for scientific progress."And India is moving forward by testing itself on this very touchstone,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Underscoring that a nation's technology creation capability and self-reliance in critical technologies depend on robust research,the spirit behind his slogan Jai Vigyan, Jai Anusandhan, the Prime Minister noted the rapid momentum of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation and recalled last year's pledge at this very forum to provide one lakh crore rupees for Research, Development, and Innovation. He highlighted that over the past year, 12,000 crore rupees committed by the government for market-ready lab technologies has been matched equally by 12,000 crore rupees from private investors. "Meaning, in just one year, a total new Commitment of 24 thousand crore rupees has been made for Research and Development,” noted PM Modi.
Spotlighting the steady expansion of the domestic research ecosystem, the Prime Minister pointed to a dramatic surge in intellectual property creation over the past decade. He noted that annual patent filings have grown from fewer than 50,000 ten years ago to nearly 1.5 lakh last year, reflecting a deeper structural shift beyond mere numbers. "They are a sign of that change in which Research and Innovation are becoming a strong Culture in India,” observed Shri Modi.
Posing a vital question for the second quarter of the 21st century on how scientific judgement will evolve in the age of AI, the Prime Minister noted that leading laboratory scientists and the Nobel Laureates on stage honed their acumen through years of solving small problems, experimenting, learning from failures, questioning established patterns, and spotting overlooked details. Warning that while AI can rapidly execute routine tasks to boost productivity, it must enrich rather than restrict independent thinking, allowing researchers to use saved time for harder problems, new experiments, and idea validation. "AI can give us answers quickly, but the responsibility of testing the veracity of the answer must lie with the scientist alone,” asserted PM Modi.
Urging continuous preparation of scientists and institutions for future-shaping domains through dedicated National Missions, spanning semiconductors, quantum technologies, biotechnology, advanced materials, robotics, space, clean energy, and next-generation communications, so that new breakthroughs emerge from India, the Prime Minister emphasized that safety and security must be prioritized across AI, synthetic biology, and autonomous systems. Warning of emerging AI-era cybersecurity threats to financial networks and national security, he called for developing AI-based and quantum security solutions that protect national systems and serve humanity. "Our goal is to develop such technologies which empower India and also contribute to solving the problems of humanity,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Calling upon every researcher, industry leader, startup founder, and student at the Conclave to set a concrete three-year target identifying which technology, prototype, pilot project, or product they will help develop, the Prime Minister urged them to drive innovations that build a Viksit Bharat and make India the global hub for solutions. He stressed that the gathering must move beyond mere discussions to deliver tangible results. "This Conclave should not remain limited merely to the exchange of ideas; may it become a platform for Measurable Outcomes,” asserted PM Modi.
Concluding his address by highlighting India's status as the world's youngest nation blessed with talent and resolve, the Prime Minister stressed the need to nurture a generation that actively leads rather than merely participates in emerging science and technology. Invoking the collective spirit and conviction of 'We will do it', he extended his best wishes for the success of the Conclave."We have to prepare such a generation which is not merely a participant in Emerging Science and Technology, but leads it,” affirmed Shri Modi.

title: English rendering of PM’s address during inauguration of the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 7:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister in my Cabinet Dr. Jitendra Singh ji, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India Ajay Sood ji, all Nobel Prize-winning scientists, all other distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen.
Today, such a large number of delegates from the world of Science and Technology are present here. Our young innovators are here as well. Before coming here, I interacted with some startup founders. The scale at which India’s youth are thinking and the confidence with which they are moving forward is truly encouraging.
Friends,
I had attended this conclave last time as well. This time, we are discussing the subject of Emerging Science and Technology. Decades ago, there was a time when Science and Technology, for India, meant catching up. Whenever something new was innovated in the world, that technology would reach us after a few years. We would adopt it or make minor improvements and move forward. But today, 21st-century India is moving ahead with a new mindset and a new confidence. Now our goal is to create new technologies for India, for the world, for today, and for the future, to determine their direction, and to develop the capability to provide solutions to global challenges. During the COVID period, we saw an example of this. When many countries around the world were struggling with vaccine availability, India developed its own vaccine, carried out vaccination on a large scale, and also supplied vaccines to other nations. This is the confidence of 21st-century India. We reach Mars in our very first attempt. We reach the South Pole of the Moon, a place where no one had reached before. And that is why I firmly believe: India must embrace the technologies of the future, innovate boldly, and lead the world in creating them.
Friends,
From the discovery of zero to the number system and astronomy, India’s tradition has always been one of knowledge and discovery. Today, we are taking this scientific heritage forward with modern technologies and renewed confidence. Some examples from the past year help us understand this transformation even better. On 30th October, the nation will celebrate the birth anniversary of Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha. Therefore, let me begin with nuclear energy.
Friends,
All of you know that for building a Developed India, we will require nuclear energy on a large scale. Dependence on imports for nuclear fuel is a challenge to our energy security. Therefore, India is rapidly advancing its Fast Breeder Reactor Technology. Just a few months ago, the country’s 500-Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor achieved First Criticality. This is an extremely significant and important step towards strengthening our long-term capabilities in the field of nuclear energy.
Friends,
Whether it is energy security or self-reliance in technology, India’s goal is not limited to fulfilling its own needs. Our objective is also to expand our strength in critical technologies. This year, India achieved new milestones in the space sector as well. An Indian space startup successfully placed a satellite into orbit using a Made-in-India rocket in its very first attempt. India also achieved the capability of satellite docking. Today, many Indian startups are bringing new solutions in space science. The participation of young scientists and entrepreneurs in the space sector is also increasing significantly.
Friends,
The range of achievements India is making across various sectors is unprecedented. This very year, India hosted the AI Impact Summit and launched its own AI model. The first shipments of chips manufactured in India have now started reaching global markets. In the field of battery storage as well, we are working on capacity building based on raw materials available within India itself.
Friends,
From nuclear energy to space, and from AI to semiconductors, the requirements of these sectors are different. But their message is one and the same. India is strengthening both its capabilities and its confidence in emerging technologies. India possesses another strength as well: solutions at scale. Whenever a solution succeeds in India, it creates pathways for solving the problems of many countries around the world. Our Digital Stack is a wonderful example of this. Our 5G technology is another example. India is moving towards developing secure solutions that can reach people on a large scale.
Friends,
You all know that one challenge in the world of Science and Technology has always been the tendency to see it as a weapon. India, however, believes that Science and Technology are instruments for the service of humanity. The true success of science comes when it moves from the laboratory into the lives of ordinary citizens and improves them. Lab to land, the success of this technology is not determined merely by how advanced it is. Its real strength lies in how large a problem it solves and how many lives it transforms. Therefore, for us, Emerging Science and Technology means solutions that strengthen healthcare, transform agriculture, create new opportunities in education and employment, and help in disaster management. I am pleased that India’s startup revolution is giving prominence to such questions. One startup is working on wearable EEG technology that helps understand brain activity. Indian companies are developing indigenous wireless and satellite communication solutions. In the field of nutrition, products are being developed keeping special dietary needs in mind. Indian companies are working on new technologies in the semiconductor sector. Solutions for utilising industrial waste such as steel slag are also being explored in our country.
Friends,
Just a few days ago, I had the opportunity to visit Chennai. I would like to share that experience with you as well. There, I inaugurated a modern Brain Centre at IIT Madras. This centre has developed a brain imaging technology platform that is a model for the entire world. This Brain Centre is working on developing high-resolution digital 3D images of the human brain. The success of this mission will help solve many complexities associated with neurological diseases. Science for Society, Technology for Transformation, this should be the benchmark of our scientific progress. And India is moving forward while measuring itself against this benchmark.
Friends,
We all know that a country’s technology and technology-creation capability depends on its research. Research is the power that enables a nation to find solutions to its own problems and become self-reliant in critical technologies. That is why I have said: Jai Vigyan, Jai Anusandhan! For a Developed India, we are continuously strengthening our research sector. With this resolve, the Anusandhan National Research Foundation is being accelerated. Last year, on this very platform, we pledged an allocation of one lakh crore rupees for Research, Development, and Innovation. Today, the results are becoming visible. In the past year, nearly twelve thousand crore rupees have already been committed to technologies that are ready to move from the laboratory to the market. And private investors are participating equally in this effort. Alongside the government’s commitment of twelve thousand crore rupees, the private sector is also investing twelve thousand crore rupees. This means that within just one year, a total new commitment of twenty-four thousand crore rupees has been made towards Research and Development.
Friends,
India’s research ecosystem is also continuously expanding. Patent applications have seen substantial growth. Ten years ago, fewer than fifty thousand patent applications were filed in an entire year. Last year, this number rose to nearly one hundred and fifty thousand. These figures do not merely indicate rising numbers. They signify a transformation in which research and innovation are emerging as a strong culture within India.
Friends,
In this second quarter of the 21st century, another question has become extremely important. In the age of AI, how will scientific judgement evolve? The scientists leading our laboratories have developed their expertise through years of experience. On this stage too, several distinguished scientists and Nobel laureates are present. We all know that they developed their understanding by solving small problems, conducting experiments, and learning from failures. A scientist does not merely repeat available information. A scientist questions established patterns. A scientist examines solutions from new perspectives. A scientist identifies aspects that others may have overlooked. It is through this process that scientific judgement develops. Today, however, in the age of AI, a new challenge is emerging before us. AI can complete many routine tasks very quickly. This can improve research productivity. But we must also ensure that AI does not limit scientific thinking and independent judgement, but instead enriches them. The time saved through AI should be used for addressing more challenging problems, conducting new experiments, and testing new ideas. AI can provide answers quickly. But the responsibility of verifying the truth of those answers must remain with the scientist.
Friends,
We must continue preparing our scientists and institutions not only for today's needs but also for future challenges. Semiconductors, Quantum Technologies, Biotechnology, Advanced Materials, Robotics, Space, Clean Energy, and Next-Generation Communications are areas that will shape the future. India is building strong scientific foundations in all these fields. For this purpose, several National Missions have also been launched. Our objective is that new breakthroughs in these domains should emerge from India as well. And our responsibility extends beyond innovation alone. Whether it is AI, synthetic biology, or autonomous systems, safety and security must be given priority. In the age of AI, new challenges and new threats are also emerging in cybersecurity. From our financial networks to our national security systems, everyone faces this challenge. Therefore, it is essential that we work on AI-based solutions and advance quantum security solutions that can secure the country’s systems against these threats. Our goal is to develop technologies that strengthen India while also contributing solutions to the challenges facing humanity.
Friends,
I appeal to every researcher, industry leader, startup founder, and young student present at this conclave to set a concrete goal for themselves. In the next three years, what technology, prototype, pilot project, or product will they contribute towards developing? Let us create innovations that support the making of a Developed India. Let us create innovations that make India a centre point for global solutions. Therefore, it is my hope that this conclave does not remain limited to an exchange of ideas alone. It should become a platform for measurable outcomes.
Friends,
Today, India is the youngest country in the world. We have talent. We have the resolve to create something new. We must build a generation that does not merely participate in Emerging Science and Technology, but leads it. Our spirit should be: We will do it. We will do it. Our confidence should be: We will do it. Once again, I extend my very best wishes for the success of this conclave.
Thank you!

title: Joint Declaration 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum New Delhi, India  26-27 October 2026
subtitle: “Fostering Parliaments for People-Centric Development”
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 5:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
We, the Presiding Officers and representatives of the Parliaments of the BRICS member countries: namely, the Federative Republic of Brazil, the People’s Republic of China, the Arab Republic of Egypt, the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, the Republic of India, the Republic of Indonesia, the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Russian Federation, the Republic of South Africa and the United Arab Emirates convened at the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum (12th BRICS PF) in New Delhi, India on 26–27 October 2026 under the theme “Fostering Parliaments For People-Centric Development”.
We extend a warm welcome for the participation of Partner countries in the 12th BRICS PF and acknowledge their invaluable contributions to inter-parliamentary cooperation. We reaffirm our commitment to fostering an inclusive, mutually beneficial, and development-oriented partnership with Partner countries, and encourage their increasing involvement in BRICS engagements and practical cooperation in areas of shared interest.
We express our support to India’s BRICS Chairship in 2026 themed: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, which reflects our shared commitment to strengthening BRICS cooperation to address common challenges in a balanced, inclusive and forward-looking manner.
We congratulate India on successfully hosting the 18th BRICS Summit from 12–13 September 2026 and welcome the adoption of the New Delhi Leaders Declaration. Furthermore, we extend our full support to India for the remainder of its BRICS Chairship in 2026.
We affirm our legislative support to strengthen the BRICS Strategic Partnership within the respective constitutional mandates and competencies of member Parliaments, across the three pillars of cooperation: political and security, economic and financial, cultural and people-to-people exchanges. We reaffirm our commitment to the BRICS spirit of mutual respect and understanding, equality, solidarity, openness, inclusiveness, and consensus.
We reiterate the significance of BRICS cultural and people-to-people exchanges and initiatives in fostering mutual understanding, friendship and cooperation amongst our nations and peoples. In this context, we welcome the organisation of key people-to-people engagements, including in the fields of culture, sport, art, education, women and youth affairs, under India’s Chairship. We call for more efforts to respect diversity of cultures, highly value inheritance, innovation and creativity, jointly advocate robust international people-to-people exchanges and cooperation and recall the adoption of the UNGA Resolution A/RES/78/286 entitled “International Day for Dialogue among Civilizations”.
We reaffirm our adherence to the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, non-intervention in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of international disputes, as enshrined in the United Nations Charter, as essential foundations for global stability, peace and development.
We recognise that inter-parliamentary cooperation constitutes an important component of the BRICS cooperation framework. It serves as a unique channel to foster mutual understanding, build trust among nations, support the peaceful resolution of international disputes, strengthen our international cooperation and promote the values of inclusiveness, solidarity, and sustainable development. In this regard, we reaffirm the role of the BRICS Parliamentary Forum and acknowledge the considerable contributions made by the eleven preceding meetings of the BRICS Parliamentary Forum in strengthening inter-parliamentary dialogue and cooperation among the Parliaments of the BRICS member countries.
We look forward to strengthening BRICS interaction within international parliamentary fora, including the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), to amplify the voice of the Global South. In this regard, we take note of Russia’s initiative to consider the idea of establishing a BRICS Plus geopolitical group within IPU.
We welcome the constructive inter-parliamentary dialogue conducted during the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum, which focused on the role of Parliaments in strengthening institutional resilience, harnessing digital technologies to address challenges faced by developing countries, fostering a more representative and inclusive global governance, promoting sustainability and accelerating collective global actions for the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including its Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
We reaffirm our commitment to diligently working towards the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its comprehensive people-centred Goals and targets in a balanced and integrated manner, aligned with national policies and regulations. We acknowledge that eradicating poverty in all its forms, including extreme poverty, is the most significant global challenge and a prerequisite for sustainable development. We further recognise the importance of promoting the 2030 Agenda in an innovative, coordinated, environmentally sound, open and shared manner. We also look forward to close cooperation and substantive contribution of BRICS Countries in shaping the global agenda for the sustainable development beyond 2030.
Recognizing the urgency of addressing climate change, we call for intensifying efforts, through dialogue and international cooperation, to implement nationally determined contributions (NDCs), strengthen mitigation and adaptation efforts, and promote just transition pathways, with a view to achieving the objectives of the UNFCCC and the goals of its Paris Agreement as applicable, while reflecting equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances. Developed countries shall provide additional, adequate, predictable, accessible financial resources, capacity building support, technology development and transfer to developing countries on mutually agreed terms for adaptation.
We acknowledge the transformative potential of Emerging Technologies, including Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs). We emphasise the necessity of ensuring the open, safe, secure, stable, equitably accessible, peaceful and interoperable use and development of ICTs environment while respecting sovereignty and national security of each country.
We recognize that Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents immense opportunity to stimulate economic growth and sustainable development for all. We further note the importance of international cooperation in enhancing equitable access to AI resources, capacity building, knowledge and opportunities in accordance with national priorities and applicable laws while ensuring the safe, secure inclusive and reliable development and use of AI. In addition, promoting energy efficiency of AI systems, fostering AI Science and Innovation, leveraging AI for economic growth and social good and mitigating potential risks would be essential for promoting a just, fair, equitable and prosperous future of all countries, especially those of Global South. We emphasize the need to strengthen the digital sovereignty of BRICS member countries by protecting data privacy and security of personal information as well as by building resilient national technological ecosystems.
We recognize the significant potential of using digital technologies and AI-driven solutions to strengthen parliamentary functions including parliamentary research, analysis, outreach, citizen interaction, and feedback. We encourage the BRICS Parliaments to share amongst each other the successful examples and best practices on the deployment of digital technologies and AI-enabled tools, in order to enable legislatures to innovate and equitably benefit from technological advancements.
We reiterate our commitment to achieving universal and meaningful connectivity for all and encourage collaborative efforts to facilitate the deployment of digital infrastructure, including digital public infrastructure, to facilitate economic development, social inclusion, improved public service delivery, and enhance resilience and innovation. In this regard, we note the proposal to launch the digital public infrastructure repository for BRICS countries and pilot projects of digital public infrastructure solutions for digital transformation for BRICS countries.
We reaffirm our commitment to reforming global governance by promoting a more just, equitable, agile, effective, efficient, responsive, representative, legitimate, democratic and accountable international and multilateral system in the spirit of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. We acknowledge that multipolarity and multilateralism can expand opportunities for Emerging Markets and Developing Countries (EMDCs) to realise their potential and enjoy universally beneficial, inclusive, sustainable and equitable economic globalization and cooperation. We highlight the importance of the Global South as a driver for positive change and reaffirm the role of BRICS in voicing its concerns and priorities, including through voluntary development cooperation and capacity-building.
We emphasize the contribution of parliamentary diplomacy, inter-parliamentary dialogue and cooperation to advancing a more representative and inclusive global governance architecture, within the respective constitutional mandates and competencies of member Parliaments.
We reiterate our commitment to the strengthening of multilateralism and upholding the international law, including the Purposes and Principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, which serve as its indispensable cornerstone. We emphasise the central role of the UN in an international system where sovereign states cooperate to maintain international peace and security, advance sustainable development, ensure the promotion and protection of democracy, human rights and fundamental freedoms for all, and foster cooperation based on solidarity, mutual respect, justice and sovereign equality while respecting national circumstances, diversity of national systems and development pathways, consistent with states’ obligations under international law with the aim to build a brighter shared future for the international community based on mutually beneficial cooperation.
We stress the urgency of reforming the current international peace and security architecture, which necessarily requires the strengthening of multilateralism, and support a comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including its Security Council. This reform should make it more just, equitable, democratic, representative, effective, and efficient, better reflecting contemporary realities and the needs of the international community. In this regard, we welcome the statement at Paragraph 13 of the BRICS New Delhi Declaration 2026.
We strongly condemn all violations of international humanitarian law, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, including in BRICS Member States, as well as the denial or obstruction of humanitarian access and the targeting of humanitarian personnel. In this regard, we take note of Paragraph 29 of the BRICS New Delhi Declaration 2026. We underline the need to address accountability for all violations of international humanitarian law. We recognize international efforts undertaken by BRICS members to promote respect for, adherence to, and effective implementation of international humanitarian law.
We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation. Furthermore, we urge to ensure the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations in their entirety and interconnectedness, including respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the States. We encourage increasing efforts, through dialogue and diplomacy, towards a long-term understanding that will contribute to lasting peace, security and stability in the region. We stress the need to work together to maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law.
We condemn the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law, and reiterate that such measures, inter alia in the form of unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far reaching negative implications on human rights, including the right to development, health and food security of the general population of targeted states. We call for the elimination of such unlawful measures which undermine international law and the principles and purposes of the UN Charter.
We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured. We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens. We reiterate that terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law. We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism. We emphasize the primary responsibility of States in combating terrorism and that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must fully comply with their obligations under international law, including the Charter of the UN, in particular the purposes and principles thereof, and relevant international conventions and protocols, in particular international human rights law, international refugee law and international humanitarian law, as applicable. We welcome the activities of the BRICS Counter-Terrorism Working Group (CTWG) and its five Subgroups based upon the BRICS Counter-Terrorism Strategy, the BRICS Counter-Terrorism Action Plan and the CTWG Position Paper. We look forward to further deepening counter-terrorism cooperation. We call for an expeditious finalization and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism in the UN framework. We call for concerted actions against all UN designated terrorists and terrorist entities.
We reaffirm our unwavering support for the peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on the two-state solution, with the two States living side by side, in peace and security, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, asserting the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, freedom, and an independent, sovereign State.
We recognize that training and capacity building are crucial for fostering effective inter-parliamentary cooperation. Therefore, we encourage the promotion of exchange of experiences, knowledge sharing and collaboration among parliamentarians and their technical and legislative advisors for capacity building and professional networking.
We take note of Russia’s proposal to consider establishing an inter-parliamentary BRICS Working Group on Sport, in line with Paragraph 8 of the Protocol to the Memorandum of Understanding on the BRICS Parliamentary Forum of 11 July 2024, which could provide a platform for the voluntary exchange of experience and best practices in the field of sport and physical education, in accordance with national laws and priorities.
On the 10th Anniversary of the BRICS Women’s Parliamentarians Forum, we recall the Jaipur Declaration of 2016, which called for the institutionalisation of this meeting as an annual event to promote more inclusive inter-parliamentary deliberations. We further encourage the strengthening of inter-parliamentary interaction through meetings of the Chairpersons of the International Affairs Committees of BRICS Parliaments, which contribute to deepening mutual understanding and facilitating the exchange of experiences and legislative best practices.
We congratulate the Parliament of India for the successful hosting of the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum and express our sincere gratitude for the hospitality extended by the Parliament and the People of India.
We look forward to reconvening in 2027 under the BRICS Chairship of the People’s Republic of China.

Reaffirming the consensus of the New Delhi Declaration (NDD), member parliaments issued an explicit endorsement of UN Security Council reform - referencing NDD Paragraph 13 - to make global governance more representative of the Global South.

The final text also strongly embedded India-led developmental and climate agendas, including the expansion of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) repositories, ethical Artificial Intelligence governance, adherence to Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC), and unanimous support for India’s BRICS Chairship.
Delivering the valedictory address, Lok Sabha Speaker emphasised that global challenges can only be resolved through steadfast dialogue, mutual peace, and collaborative action rather than conflict.

Shri Birla stressed that the success of BRICS must extend far beyond the progress of its individual member States to benefit the wider international community, granting proper representation to the aspirations of the Global South in global decision-making processes.

title: AIIA Report Indicates Encouraging Improvements in Quality of Life and Cognitive Health Among Elderly in Faridabad
subtitle: Community-based Ayurveda intervention records improvements in quality of life, Agnibala and bone mineral density; project report submitted to Expert Committee
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 2:43PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi, has reported encouraging findings from a community-based Ayurveda programme conducted in Faridabad district, Haryana, to promote the physical and mental health of elderly people. According to the project findings, improvements were recorded in quality of life, Agnibala and bone mineral density following the intervention. Positive changes were also observed in cognitive health assessments, along with improvements in selected biomarkers, including serotonin, acetylcholine, DHEA and vitamin D. The findings were presented at a workshop held at AIIA on October 24, and the project report was submitted to an expert committee.
Under its Public Health Initiative (PHI), AIIA screened 5,594 people aged 60–80 years in Faridabad district over three months and provided them with Ayurvedic medicines. In addition, under a separate component focused on dementia, 200 patients were screened and provided with Ayurveda-based medicines over four months. Titled “Community-Based Ayurveda Intervention for Promotion of Physical and Mental Health in Elderly Population of Faridabad District, Haryana State,”
the project aimed to study the potential of community-level Ayurveda-based interventions and assess approaches to promoting healthy ageing.
The initial assessment identified several health challenges among the elderly participants. These included vision-related problems in 67.73% of participants, physical inactivity in 43.05% and reduced cognitive function in 6.85%. Other concerns included high blood pressure, elevated random blood glucose levels, reduced bone mineral density, constipation and sleep-related problems.
In the first component of the project, improvements in quality of life were recorded following a 60-day intervention. The total score on the World Health Organization Quality of Life (WHOQOL) assessment increased from 292.0 to 326.3. Improvements were also observed across all six parameters used to assess Agnibala, an Ayurvedic concept associated with digestive and metabolic strength. An improvement in bone mineral density was also recorded.
In the second component, which focused on cognitive health, the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores showed a shift towards normal levels. The 6-CIT assessment also indicated signs of improved cognitive performance. The quality-of-life score in this component increased from 277.4 to 364.2. Improvements were additionally recorded in the levels of serotonin, acetylcholine (ACh), dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and vitamin D.
These findings provide a basis for further investigation into the potential of community-based Ayurveda interventions. However, more extensive scientific evaluation, continued safety monitoring and further studies are necessary to validate the findings and establish the effectiveness and safety of these interventions.
Dr. Koustubha Upadhyaya, Advisor to the Ministry of Ayush, attended the workshop as the Chief Guest, while Prof. (Vaidya) Pradeep Kumar Prajapati, Director of AIIA, presided over the programme. Dr. Upadhyaya emphasised the importance of meaningful social engagement with elderly people to better understand their needs. He also highlighted the importance of encouraging older adults to participate in physical and mental activities. In addition, he underscored the need for greater investment in such initiatives to achieve better health outcomes.
Prof. (Vaidya) Prajapati appreciated the efforts of the Public Health Initiative team and stressed the importance of systematically studying experiences with community-based Ayurveda healthcare services and widely disseminating the findings. He also emphasised the need to extend such initiatives to a larger number of elderly people. The Director further emphasised the importance of the joint family system, highlighting its role in ensuring proper care, support, and emotional well-being of the elderly.
The workshop also featured contributions from Dr. Suneela Garg, Director Professor and Head of the Department of Community Medicine at Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi; Dr. Suman Ray, Senior Principal Scientist at the CSIR–National Institute of Science Communication and Policy Research (NIScPR); and Dr. Lokesh Singh Shekhawat, Professor of Psychiatry at Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.
The occasion also witnessed the release of the book
Holistic Approach for Healthy Aging
. Other attendees included Prof. (Dr.) Manjusha Rajagopala, Dean (DU); Prof. (Dr.) Mahesh Vyas, Dean (Ph.D.); Prof. (Dr.) R. K. Yadav, Dean (PG); and Prof. (Dr.) Yogesh Badwe, Medical Superintendent, along with other faculty members of the institute.
The All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi, is an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India. The institute works to advance Ayurveda through education, research, clinical services and public health initiatives.

title: ICAR-MGIFRI Promotes Soil Health, Balanced Fertilisation and Sustainable Orchard Management under Khet Bachao Abhiyan 2026
subtitle: Farmer awareness programme in East Champaran highlights nutrient recycling, crop diversification and resource-efficient mango and litchi cultivation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 2:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The ICAR–Mahatma Gandhi Integrated Farming Research Institute (ICAR-MGIFRI), Motihari, Bihar under the Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) organised a farmer awareness and field interaction programme under Khet Bachao Abhiyan 2026 at Kothia Hariram village in Mehsi Block of East Champaran on 27th October, 2026. The programme focused on promoting balanced fertilisation, soil health management, nutrient recycling, crop diversification and sustainable management of mango and litchi orchards. A total of 29 farmers and participants attended the programme and interacted with scientists on practical approaches to improving orchard productivity and resource-use efficiency.
The programme was led by Dr. Amol K. Jadhav, Scientist, ICAR-MGIFRI, who emphasised the importance of soil-test-based nutrient management and balanced fertilisation for maintaining orchard productivity and long-term soil fertility. He explained that indiscriminate fertiliser application can increase cultivation costs and cause nutrient imbalances, whereas fertiliser use based on soil-test results, crop requirements and orchard conditions can improve nutrient-use efficiency and support sustainable production.
During the interaction, farmers were sensitised to nutrient recycling and the effective utilisation of locally available organic resources, including crop residues, fallen leaves, farmyard manure and compost. Dr. Jadhav explained that recycling these materials can improve soil organic matter, support better soil structure and nutrient availability, and reduce dependence on external inputs. He also highlighted the importance of combining organic resources with balanced mineral fertilisation for sustainable mango and litchi cultivation.
The programme highlighted the potential of intercropping and crop diversification in fruit orchards to improve land-use efficiency and create supplementary income opportunities. Farmers were encouraged to consider suitable intercrops, particularly legumes and other location-specific crops, according to orchard age, canopy coverage, seasonal moisture availability and crop compatibility. These practices can help utilise available resources more efficiently while diversifying farm income.
Participating farmers shared their experiences and challenges concerning fertiliser application, orchard soil health, organic resource management and intercropping. The interactive discussions helped raise awareness of practical, economically viable and environmentally sustainable approaches to improving the productivity and profitability of fruit-based farming systems.

date:

content:
The Ministry of Civil Aviation, under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Civil Aviaation Shri Samir Kumar Sinha, held the first Fog Preparedness Meeting for the upcoming winter season to review preparedness and coordination among stakeholders for the fog season 26-27. The meeting was attended by the Director General, DGCA Shri Vir Vikram Yadav; Chairman, Airports Authority of India (AAI) Shri Puneet Kansal; senior officials from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS); Central Industrial Security Force (CISF); India Meteorological Department (IMD) along with representatives of Delhi Airport & other fog-affected airports and airlines.
The IMD officials stated that the fog season is expected to run from 15 December
2026 to 15 February
2027. The meeting focused on ensuring smooth airport operations and minimising inconvenience to passengers during fog-related disruptions. Emphasis was laid on advance preparedness, timely communication, effective coordination among stakeholders and appropriate assistance to passengers in case of flight delays, cancellations and rescheduling.
The DGCA was emphasised to ensure regulatory oversight, compliance with applicable instructions, verification of aircraft and crew preparedness, and effective passenger facilitation measures by airlines. The AAI and airport operators were directed to ensure the readiness of Instrument Landing Systems (ILS) and Runway Visual Range (RVR) systems, airside safety, adequate terminal capacity and effective coordination for airport operations during low-visibility conditions.
Airlines were directed to ensure the availability of qualified crew and compliant aircraft for low visibility operations, plan realistic flight schedules and take timely decisions regarding flight operations. It was emphasised that passengers should receive timely updates through SMS, mobile applications and email regarding delays, cancellations and revised departure times, so that they don’t reach the airport without adequate information about their flights.
The IMD was directed to ensure reliable weather forecasts, regular observations and timely dissemination of weather updates to facilitate operational planning. Air Traffic Control and air navigation service providers were instructed to ensure safe sequencing of air traffic, adherence to low-visibility procedures and coordinated traffic management during fog conditions.
The role of BCAS and CISF in ensuring safe and orderly passenger movement, including terminal re-entry and re-boarding wherever required, was also discussed. Airlines were directed to ensure that their respective ground handlers maintain adequate staffing, ensure efficient baggage management and aircraft turnaround, and provide necessary assistance to passengers during operational disruptions.

Preparations to be made to ensure adequate staffing at check-in counters, airline helpdesks and customer care facilities. Secretary emphasised that airlines need to ensure that their helpline desks at the airports are manned by informed and empowered personnel who can adequately address the queries of the passengers.
The meeting underscored the importance of coordinated efforts by all stakeholders to ensure safe and efficient operations during the fog season. The collective objective is to minimise passenger inconvenience through advance preparedness, timely information, clear operational decisions and effective passenger assistance during the upcoming fog season.

The year 2026 marks the completion of ten years of the Startup India initiative, launched in January 2016 to build a strong, inclusive and innovation-driven entrepreneurial ecosystem in the country. Since its inception in 2019, the National Startup Awards have emerged as a flagship initiative under Startup India, providing a national platform to recognise entrepreneurial excellence and showcase innovative solutions addressing critical challenges across sectors.
The National Startup Awards recognise startups demonstrating outstanding performance in innovation, scalability, sustainability and socio-economic impact. Building upon the success of the previous five editions, NSA 6.0 seeks to strengthen India’s startup ecosystem by encouraging innovation-led entrepreneurship, fostering inclusive participation and promoting globally competitive startups.

Introduced for the first time, the student award aims to foster a culture of innovation and entrepreneurship among school and college students across all 36 States and Union Territories. DPIIT will engage Central Ministries and Departments, State and UT Governments, incubators, academic institutions, banks and financial institutions, Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), industry associations and other ecosystem stakeholders to support outreach, participation and evaluation under the awards.

title: DPIIT Advances Trust-Based Governance Through Startup Support, Regulatory Reforms and Digital Single-Window Clearances
subtitle:
Startup India Supports 2.5 Lakh+ Startups, Generating 25.42 Lakh+ Jobs Across 770+ Districts

Startup Credit Guarantees Reach ₹1,662 Crore as 63 Regulatory Reforms Strengthen the Startup Ecosystem

47,957 Compliances Reduced and 900 Legal Provisions Decriminalised to Ease Business Regulations Across India

Labour Law Consolidation and Licensing Reforms Simplify Compliance and Reduce Regulatory Burden on Businesses

India Records USD 843 Billion in FDI Over 12 Years as Investment Reforms Expand Automatic Route Across 17 Sectors

National Single Window System Simplifies Approvals Through Digital Integration, Automation and 22-Language Accessibility
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 12:24PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, has driven a sustained shift from a permission-based to a trust-based regulatory framework. Reforms across the startup ecosystem, compliance reduction, sectoral regulation, foreign direct investment and single-window clearances have reduced the regulatory burden on businesses and delivered measurable outcomes in business entry, employment, investment and digital service delivery.
DPIIT has recognised 2,50,046 startups, reporting over 25.42 lakh jobs across 770+ districts and 56 industries. Of these startups, 52% are from non-metro cities and 48% have at least one woman director. Annual recognitions increased from 34,200 in FY 2023-24 to 36,440 in FY 2024-25.
Under the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, ₹775.67 crore has been approved for 4,194 startups across 32 States/UTs through 244 incubators, including 2,147 women-led startups and 2,356 startups from Tier-II and Tier-III cities. Under the Fund of Funds for Startups, SIDBI has committed ₹12,623 crore to 166 Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), which have invested ₹28,254 crore in 1,475 startups.
The Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups has guaranteed 532 loans worth ₹1,662.71 crore to startups employing 41,637 people. The guarantee cover per borrower has been doubled from ₹10 crore to ₹20 crore, while the annual fee has been reduced to 1% for 27 Champion Sectors.
A total of 63 regulatory reforms have been enabled, including the abolition of angel tax, harmonisation of long-term capital gains taxation for listed and unlisted shares, and permission for insurance companies, EPFO, superannuation funds and gratuity funds to invest in AIFs. Further, 4,467 startups hold the Section 80-IAC certificate of eligibility.
With prior-experience, prior-turnover and Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) requirements relaxed, the number of startups registered on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) has increased from 7,929 in January 2021 to 43,260. These startups have delivered 6.23 lakh orders worth ₹68,105 crore to public buyers. Dedicated startup policies have expanded from four States/UTs in 2016 to 32. In addition, 104 new incubators have been established across 17 States/UTs, while the TEJAS initiative covers 132 districts in 27 States/UTs.
A total of 47,957 compliances have been reduced across Central Ministries and States/UTs. Of these, 22,290 have been digitised, 16,141 simplified, 5,255 decriminalised and 4,271 eliminated. The Jan Vishwas Acts have decriminalised 900 provisions of Central laws, comprising 183 provisions across 42 Acts in 2023 and 717 provisions across 79 Acts in 2026.
States/UTs have implemented over 9,700 reforms across seven editions of the Business Reforms Action Plan (BRAP). The District BRAP extends 222 reforms to District Collectorates, Development Authorities and Urban Local Bodies.
Twenty-nine Central labour laws have been consolidated into four Labour Codes. The threshold for prior permission for lay-off or closure has been raised from 100 to 300 workers. The applicability threshold for factories has been increased from 10 to 20 workers for establishments using power and from 20 to 40 workers for those not using power. The threshold for contract-labour licensing has been raised from 20 to 50 workers. A 30-day compliance notice is now mandatory before legal action.
The validity of licences issued by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO) has been extended from five to ten years, reducing the need for renewals. All PESO modules have been digitised and integrated with the National Single Window System (NSWS), with online No Objection Certificates (NOCs) issued by District Authorities and fee relaxations provided for women and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). The Boilers Act, 2025, has replaced the colonial-era Boilers Act, 1923.
Seventeen sectors have moved to the automatic route for foreign direct investment (FDI). In the defence sector, the FDI limit under the automatic route has been raised from 49% to 74% for new industrial licences. The FDI limit in insurance was raised from 49% to 74% in 2021 and to 100% in 2026 for insurers investing their entire premium in India. The sector attracted approximately USD 8.79 billion in FDI from FY 2021-22 to FY 2024-25.
Up to 100% FDI is permitted under the automatic route in telecommunications, non-scheduled air transport services and ground handling in civil aviation, as well as satellite component manufacturing and broadcasting distribution.
India received USD 843 billion in FDI during FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26, 169% higher than the USD 313 billion received in the preceding twelve years. The inflow reached an all-time high of USD 94.53 billion in FY 2025-26.
The National Single Window System (NSWS) has received 15,49,850 applications, registered 5,76,778 businesses and delivered over 8.5 lakh approvals. A total of 3,779 services are live on the platform, comprising 327 Central and 3,452 State services, compared with 142 Central approvals and 14 States/UTs at its soft launch in September 2021. The system has integrated 34 States/UTs and 32 Central Ministries/Departments, with 18 Central Ministries using NSWS.
The Know Your Approvals (KYA) module enables businesses to identify the Central and State approvals applicable to them at the outset, providing visibility of over 8,000 approvals. Of these, 2,825 approvals, comprising 592 Central and 2,233 State approvals, are integrated through KYA. To eliminate repetitive data entry, 89 common data fields now auto-populate across 285 approvals. The portal is available in 22 Indian languages, improving accessibility for entrepreneurs across regions.
NSWS is also being used to eliminate approval steps altogether. The Industrial Entrepreneur Memorandum (IEM) is now auto-generated using data drawn from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) and other databases, without requiring departmental approval. Similarly, e-B4 production visa sponsorship letters for foreign professionals are generated through API integration between NSWS and the Visa portal, without requiring approval from the concerned line Ministry.
States/UTs have been encouraged to establish and strengthen Single Window Systems (SWS) as integrated digital platforms providing businesses with a single point of access to regulatory approvals and compliances. The framework promotes features such as Single Sign-On, Single Business ID, Know Your Approvals, Common Application Forms, online payments, inspection management, applicant guidance, grievance redressal and real-time dashboards, supported by inter-departmental integration and end-to-end digital processing.
These initiatives aim to reduce procedural complexity, minimise physical touchpoints, improve transparency and ensure time-bound service delivery. Taken together, the reforms mark a steady transition towards simpler, digital and less burdensome regulation, enabling businesses to start, grow and invest with greater ease.

title: Ministry of Culture signs MoU with Bibliothèque nationale de France to strengthen preservation of India’s manuscript heritage
subtitle: Collaboration to focus on digitisation, digital access, technology exchange, conservation and research on Indic-origin manuscripts
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 7:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed and exchanged on 26 October 2026 in Paris between the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF) (National Library of France), under Gyan Bharatam Mission, to strengthen institutional cooperation in the preservation, digitisation, research and dissemination of manuscript and documentary heritage. The MoU was signed by Shri Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and Mr Gilles Pécout, President of BnF.
Shri Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and Gilles Pécout, President of Bibliothèque nationale de France
The partnership brings together the Ministry of Culture, through Gyan Bharatam, National Archives of India, New Delhi, and National Library, Kolkata, and BnF. It establishes a framework for cooperation across five key areas: Digitisation; Cross-Sharing on the National Digital Repository; Technology Exchange; Conservation; and Research & Development.
The Ministry of Culture and BnF will work to identify and digitise Indic-origin manuscripts and collections held by BnF. The MoU further provides for exchange of expertise and knowledge in areas such as digitisation and preservation technologies, cataloguing standards, OCR/HTR tools for Indian scripts, digital humanities and manuscript conservation. Joint workshops, capacity-building programmes, research initiatives, publications, exhibitions and exchanges of scholars and experts have also been envisaged under the partnership.
Gyan Bharatam Mission is the Ministry of Culture's flagship initiative dedicated to the identification, documentation, conservation, digitisation, translation, research and dissemination of India's manuscript heritage. Its National Digital Repository is envisaged as a secure digital repository for Indian-origin manuscripts and Indian Knowledge Systems held in India and across the world, enabling structured, permission-based access for research and study.
Bridging centuries of knowledge and heritage, the partnership marks an important step towards strengthening international cooperation for the preservation, study and wider dissemination of India’s manuscript heritage, while creating new opportunities for scholarly and technological collaboration.

title: Union Education Minister Shri Pralhad Joshi Inaugurates CBSE Experience Centre in New Delhi
subtitle:
Experience Centre to Promote Experiential Learning and Future-Ready Education

Fostering curiosity, creativity and confidence among students is essential to realise the vision of a developed India by 2047: Shri Pralhad Joshi
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 8:30PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Education, Shri Pralhad Joshi, today inaugurated the CBSE Experience Centre at the CBSE Integrated Complex, Dwarka, New Delhi. Established at CBSE headquarters, the Centre offers students an immersive learning environment taking them beyond textbooks. It provides an opportunity to explore the evolution of education, engage with emerging technologies, and gain insights into future career opportunities.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Pralhad Joshi emphasised on the need to move beyond rote learning and an excessive focus on examination scores towards an education system that recognised students’ individual interests, abilities and learning capacities. He highlighted that learning should extend beyond textbooks and enable students to understand concepts, apply their knowledge and develop confidence through real-life experiences.
The Minister said that the CBSE Experience Centre reflected the objectives of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasised on experiential and holistic learning. He noted that such initiatives could nurture curiosity, encourage independent thinking and creativity, and prepare students to face challenges with greater confidence.
Highlighting the importance of practical learning, the Minister emphasised that students should not merely study scientific concepts but also observe, experiment, and understand them through hands-on experiences. Referring to the role of Atal Tinkering Labs in encouraging innovation and scientific temper, he stated that 10,000 Atal Tinkering Labs were already operational across the country, and that the government had decided to establish 50,000 additional labs.
Shri Pralhad Joshi observed that education should equip young people with the knowledge, skills and values required to contribute meaningfully to society and the nation’s development. Emphasising on India’s growing potential in technology, manufacturing and innovation, he underscored the need to prepare students for the evolving demands of the global workforce. Referring to the recently launched Seva First Innovation Challenge, the Minister noted that opportunities for practical experimentation and problem-solving can help nurture the next generation of innovators.
The Minister also expressed confidence that the Experience Centre would contribute to making school education more engaging, practical and student-centred. He emphasised that fostering curiosity, creativity and confidence among students was essential for preparing future generations to contribute to the vision of a developed India by 2047.
The CBSE Experience Centre will take visitors through the changing story of education in India. It connects ancient traditions with modern learning and new career opportunities. The Centre houses 12 broad zones and 21 exhibits spread across 6,000 square feet. RFID-enabled smart cards allow visitors to interact with the exhibits, participate in activities and access personalised takeaways and game-based leaderboards.
The experience opens with
‘Shiksha Ki Kahani’
, a film narrated using a representational voice personifying river Saraswati. It traces the evolution of knowledge and education in India, from the gurukul system and historic learning centres like Nalanda to modern schools and digital classrooms. It also highlights the role of today's students in taking forward this legacy and contributing to the Viksit Bharat’s vision.
A special section tracks the rise of CBSE through historical photographs and archival material. This includes records from the year 1935 and provides a glimpse into the role of the Board in the evolution of the school education system. The Centre also introduces students to the history of Earth through a
Visual and Interactive Geological timeline
spanning millions of years.
The Centre will also introduce students to career exploration. Interactive exhibits such as
‘Career Explorer’
,
‘Future of Professions’
and
‘Magic Mirror: Future You’
will enable visitors to explore different career options and understand how the nature of work may change in the years ahead. The experience also includes
holographic interactions with eminent personalities including Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and Dr. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam.
A
dedicated kiosk on ‘Exam Warriors’, the book by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi
focuses on encouraging students to develop a healthier approach to examinations. It highlights the importance of confidence, stress management and a positive attitude.
The Centre's final experience,
‘Eduverse’
, combines motion-based interaction and multisensory elements. It will take visitors across various natural landscapes, from forests, oceans and the Himalayas to the Moon and other planets. It returns to Earth with a simple but important message: natural systems are interconnected, and every individual is part of this living planet.

title: India Reaffirms Commitment to Biodiversity Conservation and Effective Implementation of Global Biodiversity Framework at CBD COP-17 at Yerevan, Armenia
subtitle: Shri Bhupender Yadav emphasizes importance of National Circumstances and Adequate Means of Implementation in Science-based Biodiversity Governance
ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 OCT 2026 2:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, today delivered India’s National Statement at the High-Level Segment of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP-17) in Yerevan, Armenia. The Minister reaffirmed India’s commitment to conserving biodiversity and strengthening collective efforts to live in harmony with nature. He appreciated the Government of Armenia for hosting the seventeenth meeting of the CBD.
Shri Yadav emphasized that implementation of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework must be aligned with national priorities, circumstances and legislation, and supported by adequate and predictable finance, capacity-building and technology transfer from developed countries. India also supports benefit-sharing from digital sequence information on genetic resources through the multilateral mechanism, including the Cali Fund. The Minister advocated a science-based, risk-proportionate and precautionary approach to synthetic biology and biosafety. India’s updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan translates the Global Biodiversity Framework into 23 National Biodiversity Targets and 142 indicators, he informed.
Highlighting India’s progress in biodiversity conservation, Shri Yadav stated that the country has 1,134 Protected Areas, 103 Ramsar sites, 57 Biodiversity Heritage Sites and 18 Biosphere Reserves, including 13 under UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere Network. He highlighted that under the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the International Big Cat Alliance is advancing international cooperation for conservation of the world’s seven big-cat species and their habitats. The Mission LiFE and Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam further underlines environmental stewardship and make biodiversity conservation a collective societal endeavour, he added.
The Minister informed that India is also advancing biodiversity conservation and ecosystem restoration through initiatives including the Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes (MISHTI) for mangrove restoration, Amrit Dharohar for wetland conservation, and the Soil Health Card Scheme for sustainable soil management and maintaining soil fertility. Shri Yadav highlighted that India has aligned its legislation with the Convention and established village-level committees for decentralised access and benefit sharing, enabling local participation and benefits from sustainable biological resource use.
Reaffirming India’s commitment to multilateral cooperation, Shri Yadav said that India would continue to work with all Parties to advance the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in the true spirit of “One Earth, One Family, One Future”.
